entries.title: When Jorge Luis Borges Co-Wrote a Surreal Sci-Fi Noir Film: Invasión (1969)
entries.summary: “La ciudad es más que la gente.” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión, the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal […]
entries.content:
“La ciu­dad es más que la gente.” So declares a char­ac­ter called Don Por­firio in Invasión, the debut fea­ture by Argen­tine direc­tor Hugo San­ti­a­go. The line is the film’s most mem­o­rable, not least because of the rever­sal it pulls on our expec­ta­tions. Say­ing that a city is real­ly its peo­ple must have been a some­what banal obser­va­tion even in 1969, when Invasión came out, but say­ing that a city is more than its peo­ple still sounds con­trar­i­an enough to be intrigu­ing. It’s even more com­pelling com­ing from Don Por­firio, a mas­ter­mind whose intense­ly abstract­ed man­ner and refined lit­er­ary dic­tion will remind some view­ers of no fig­ure so much as Jorge Luis Borges — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

Anoth­er major con­trib­u­tor to Invasión’s screen­play was Borges’ long­time friend, occa­sion­al col­lab­o­ra­tor, and junior col­league in let­ters Adol­fo Bioy Casares. Any­one who’s read about their rela­tion­ship (as detailed in Bioy Casares’ tome of pub­lished diaries, sim­ply titled Borges) knows how deeply entan­gled it was with the streets of Buenos Aires, where both of them were born and raised. And any­one who knows Buenos Aires will rec­og­nize those streets onscreen in this film, despite the title card that calls it Aquilea. Echo­ing the name of Achilles, it offers a clue as to Borges and Bioy Casares’ clas­si­cal inspi­ra­tion for this project, which trans­pos­es the city under siege of Home­r’s Troy into mid-cen­tu­ry Latin Amer­i­ca, where a small group of resis­tance mem­bers orga­nize against an arriv­ing army of men­ac­ing white-coat­ed invaders.

Though Borges was­n’t exact­ly one for top­i­cal­i­ty in his own fic­ciones, it would­n’t be whol­ly unrea­son­able to make an alle­gor­i­cal read­ing of the film. It’s set in the year 1957, when Argenti­na was ruled by Pedro Euge­nio Aram­bu­ru, one of sev­er­al dic­ta­tors in the coun­try’s twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry his­to­ry. It came out dur­ing the dic­ta­tor­ship of Juan Car­los Onganía Car­ballo. And the 1976 mil­i­tary coup that put Jorge Rafael Videla in pow­er ban­ished it to an offi­cial non-exis­tence, seen only in the most under­ground screen­ings. It was­n’t until the nine­teen-nineties that Invasión was redis­cov­ered and made whole out of par­tial prints found in France, the coun­try to which San­ti­a­go had long since decamped. Now it can be seen on YouTube in one ver­sion with option­al Eng­lish and French sub­ti­tles, and anoth­er, high­er res­o­lu­tion ver­sion with French sub­ti­tles only.

View­ers today may be quick to notice the obvi­ous bud­getary lim­i­ta­tions, man­i­fest in odd-sound­ing foley work and the­atri­cal death scenes, but the cin­e­mat­ic vital­i­ty of its mix­ture of film noir, Nou­velle Vague, polit­i­cal thriller, and even sci­ence fic­tion remains unde­ni­able. (With the chas­es and explo­sions it man­ages, it may even par­tial­ly qual­i­fy as an action movie.) So does the atmos­phere of the real loca­tions — the streets Borges and Bioy Casares walked, as well as cafés, rail yards, and the cli­mac­tic foot­ball sta­di­um — that con­sti­tute its alter­nate­ly state­ly and des­o­late set­ting. It would be clichéd to say that the city itself becomes a char­ac­ter, but it would also prompt us to ask, which city, Buenos Aires or Aquilea? As with so many oth­er ques­tions about Invasión, there is no one answer.

entries.title: Watch Accurate Recreations of Medieval Italian Longsword Fighting Techniques, All Based on a Manuscript from 1404
entries.summary: Given recent history, the prospect of hundreds of young men meeting on Facebook, then traveling from around the country to a central U.S. location might sound like reasonable cause for alarm. Yet a convention fitting that description had nothing to do with political violence but, rather, a celebration and appreciation of the name “Josh” (full disclosure: […]
entries.content:
Giv­en recent his­to­ry, the prospect of hun­dreds of young men meet­ing on Face­book, then trav­el­ing from around the coun­try to a cen­tral U.S. loca­tion might sound like rea­son­able cause for alarm. Yet a con­ven­tion fit­ting that descrip­tion had noth­ing to do with polit­i­cal vio­lence but, rather, a cel­e­bra­tion and appre­ci­a­tion of the name “Josh” (full dis­clo­sure: this writer did not attend). The gath­er­ing of the Josh­es in April 2021 in Nebras­ka could not have been more peace­ful, includ­ing its fin­ish­ing bat­tle royale, con­duct­ed with pool noo­dles.

The Josh­es had no con­cern for prop­er pool-noo­dle-wield­ing tech­nique, if there is such a thing. But groups of peo­ple who gath­er around the coun­try to stage medieval-style bat­tles in live-action role play­ing (LARP) games with weapons both real and fake might ben­e­fit from point­ers.

So, too, might those who chore­o­graph sword fights on stage and screen. Where can seri­ous his­tor­i­cal re-cre­ators learn how to wield a real blade in his­tor­i­cal­ly accu­rate com­bat? One resource can be found at Wik­te­nauer, a wiki devot­ed to col­lect­ing “all of the pri­ma­ry and sec­ondary source lit­er­a­ture that makes up the text of his­tor­i­cal Euro­pean Mar­tial arts (HEMA) research.”

The Fior di Battaglia (“Flower of Bat­tle”)—an Ital­ian fenc­ing man­u­al by Fiore de’i Liberi dat­ing from cir­ca 1404—offers rich­ly- and copi­ous­ly-illus­trat­ed demon­stra­tions of medieval Ital­ian longsword fight­ing tech­niques. In the orig­i­nal man­u­script, seen here and at The Get­ty, “the illus­tra­tions are inked sketch­es with gold leaf­ing on the crowns and garters,” notes the Wik­te­nauer entry. They dom­i­nate the text, which “takes the form of descrip­tive para­graphs set in poor Ital­ian verse, which are nev­er­the­less fair­ly clear and infor­ma­tive.” So clear, indeed, the brood­ing young men of Akademia Szermierzy—a Pol­ish group that recre­ates medieval sword-fight­ing techniques—can more than con­vinc­ing­ly mim­ic the moves in the video at the top.

Once they get going, after some req­ui­site pre-fight rig­ma­role, it’s impres­sive stuff, maybe already famil­iar to mod­ern fencers and cer­tain mem­bers of the Soci­ety for Cre­ative Anachro­nism, the LARP-ing orga­ni­za­tion of ama­teurs recre­at­ing every­thing from the Mid­dle Ages and the Renais­sance. But for those who think all live-action role-play­ing is the equiv­a­lent of the Bat­tle of the Josh­es (or off-brand Nazis run­ning through the streets in home­made armor), the sheer bal­let of his­tor­i­cal sword-fight­ing may come as a sur­prise — and maybe inspire a few more peo­ple to pull on the dou­blet and hose. See more medieval sword-fight­ing recre­ations from Akademia Szer­mierzy here, and the full text of the Fior di Battaglia here.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2021.

Relat­ed Con­tent:

entries.title: Behold the Gloriously Cheap 1970s Italian Knockoffs Inspired by Star Wars
entries.summary: When the first Star Wars movie came out, in 1977, cinema was the better part of a century old, yet it had never produced a popular-culture phenomenon on such a scale. Covering the resulting explosion of public enthusiasm, the contemporary media initially struggled to find ways to describe the picture itself. “A cowboy movie set […]
entries.content:
When the first Star Wars movie came out, in 1977, cin­e­ma was the bet­ter part of a cen­tu­ry old, yet it had nev­er pro­duced a pop­u­lar-cul­ture phe­nom­e­non on such a scale. Cov­er­ing the result­ing explo­sion of pub­lic enthu­si­asm, the con­tem­po­rary media ini­tial­ly strug­gled to find ways to describe the pic­ture itself. “A cow­boy movie set in space, that’s Star Wars,” pro­nounces the announc­er in a TV news clip includ­ed in the new Nerd­writer video above. “It’s old-fash­ioned escapist enter­tain­ment, pure and sim­ple.” That may have been all the Ital­ian film indus­try need­ed to hear. The “spaghet­ti west­erns” of the pre­vi­ous dozen years had proven that it could prof­itably mas­ter an Amer­i­can genre; sure­ly it could do the same with a sim­i­lar one.

Among the results, alas, one looks in vain for A Fist­ful of Dol­lars, or even a Nava­jo Joe. Nerd­writer cre­ator Evan Puschak goes over var­i­ous instances of shame­less imi­ta­tion that char­ac­ter­ize the Ital­ian Star Wars clones, but you don’t have to take his word for it; you can, in fact, find some of these movies on YouTube.

Lui­gi Cozzi’s Star­Crash, for exam­ple, stars David Has­sel­hoff, The Spy Who Loved Me Bond girl Car­o­line Munro, and a Christo­pher Plum­mer putting in one of his most grandiose­ly vil­lain­ous per­for­mances ever; Aldo Lado’s The Humanoid, an even more shame­less knock-off, cred­its its direc­tor as “George B. Lewis.” Nor was Italy the only coun­try cash­ing in on the Star Wars craze: Puschak also shows clips from the Japan­ese film Mes­sage From Space by no less an auteur than Bat­tle Royale direc­tor Kin­ji Fukasaku.

Though many of these sec­ond-rate (at best) space operas made mon­ey, and some have even retained a cer­tain charm near­ly 50 years lat­er, they all come up against the fun­da­men­tal stingi­ness of the Cinecit­tà pro­duc­tion mod­el. “The truth is that you can’t imi­tate Star Wars with a low bud­get,” says Puschak. Despite all that’s been said about the myr­i­ad ways in which it taps into the pow­er of uni­ver­sal myth, “the spec­ta­cle, the immer­sion induced by its ground­break­ing spe­cial effects, was just as vital to the expe­ri­ence as the sto­ry and the char­ac­ters.” Hard as it may be for today’s young view­ers to believe, there was a time when movie­go­ers weren’t all that dis­crim­i­nat­ing about the real­ism, or even the plau­si­bil­i­ty, of the visu­als onscreen. After Star Wars, for bet­ter or for worse, they’d nev­er over­look vis­i­ble wires, unsteady lip-sync, or flat mat­te paint­ings so eas­i­ly again.

Relat­ed Con­tent:

entries.title: How Leo Tolstoy Became a Vegetarian and Jumpstarted the Vegetarian & Humanitarian Movements in the 19th Century
entries.summary: Leo Tolstoy is remembered as both a towering pinnacle of Russian literature and a fascinating example of Christian anarchism, a mystical version of which the aristocratic author pioneered in the last quarter century of his life. After a dramatic conversion, Tolstoy rejected his social position, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits […]
entries.content:
Leo Tol­stoy is remem­bered as both a tow­er­ing pin­na­cle of Russ­ian lit­er­a­ture and a fas­ci­nat­ing exam­ple of Chris­t­ian anar­chism, a mys­ti­cal ver­sion of which the aris­to­crat­ic author pio­neered in the last quar­ter cen­tu­ry of his life. After a dra­mat­ic con­ver­sion, Tol­stoy reject­ed his social posi­tion, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits of his cul­ture, becom­ing a vocal pro­po­nent of veg­e­tar­i­an­ism in his ascetic quest for the good life. Thou­sands of his con­tem­po­raries found Tolstoy’s exam­ple deeply com­pelling, and sev­er­al com­munes formed around his prin­ci­ples, to his dis­may. “To speak of ‘Tol­stoy­ism,’” he wrote, “to seek guid­ance, to inquire about my solu­tion of ques­tions, is a great and gross error.”

“Still,” writes Kelsey Osgood at The New York­er, “peo­ple insist­ed on seek­ing guid­ance from him,” includ­ing a young Mahat­ma Gand­hi, who struck up a live­ly cor­re­spon­dence with the writer and in 1910 found­ed a com­mu­ni­ty called “Tol­stoy Farm” near Johan­nes­burg.

Though uneasy in the role of move­ment leader, the author of Anna Karen­i­na invit­ed such treat­ment by pub­lish­ing dozens of philo­soph­i­cal and the­o­log­i­cal works, many of them in oppo­si­tion to a con­trary strain of reli­gious and moral ideas devel­op­ing in the late nine­teenth cen­tu­ry. Often called “mus­cu­lar Chris­tian­i­ty,” this trend respond­ed to what many Vic­to­ri­ans thought of as a cri­sis of mas­culin­i­ty by empha­siz­ing sports and war­rior ideals and rail­ing against the “fem­i­niza­tion” of the cul­ture.

Tol­stoy might be said to rep­re­sent a “veg­etable Christianity”—seeking har­mo­ny with nature and turn­ing away from all forms of vio­lence, includ­ing the eat­ing of meat. In “The First Step,” an 1891 essay on diet and eth­i­cal com­mit­ment, he char­ac­ter­ized the pre­vail­ing reli­gious atti­tude toward food:

I remem­ber how, with pride at his orig­i­nal­i­ty, an Evan­gel­i­cal preach­er, who was attack­ing monas­tic asceti­cism, once said to me “Ours is not a Chris­tian­i­ty of fast­ing and pri­va­tions, but of beef­steaks.” Chris­tian­i­ty, or virtue in general—and beef­steaks!

While he con­fessed him­self “not hor­ri­fied by this asso­ci­a­tion,” it is only because “there is no bad odor, no sound, no mon­stros­i­ty, to which man can­not become so accus­tomed that he ceas­es to remark what would strike a man unac­cus­tomed to it.” The killing and eat­ing of ani­mals, Tol­stoy came to believe, is a hor­ror to which—like war and serfdom—his cul­ture had grown far too accus­tomed. Like many an ani­mal rights activist today, Tol­stoy con­veyed his hor­ror of meat-eat­ing by describ­ing a slaugh­ter­house in detail, con­clud­ing:

[I]f he be real­ly and seri­ous­ly seek­ing to live a good life, the first thing from which he will abstain will always be the use of ani­mal food, because, to say noth­ing of the exci­ta­tion of the pas­sions caused by such food, its use is sim­ply immoral, as it involves the per­for­mance of an act which is con­trary to the moral feeling—killing.

[W]e can­not pre­tend that we do not know this. We are not ostrich­es, and can­not believe that if we refuse to look at what we do not wish to see, it will not exist.… [Y]oung, kind, unde­praved people—especially women and girls—without know­ing how it log­i­cal­ly fol­lows, feel that virtue is incom­pat­i­ble with beef­steaks, and, as soon as they wish to be good, give up eat­ing flesh.

The idea of veg­e­tar­i­an­ism of course pre­ced­ed Tol­stoy by hun­dreds of years of Hin­du and Bud­dhist prac­tice. And its grow­ing pop­u­lar­i­ty in Europe and Amer­i­ca pre­ced­ed him as well. “Tol­stoy became an out­spo­ken veg­e­tar­i­an at the age of 50,” writes Sam Pavlenko, “after meet­ing the pos­i­tivist and veg­e­tar­i­an William Frey, who, accord­ing to Tolstoy’s son Sergei Lvovich, vis­it­ed the great writer in the autumn of 1885.” Tolstoy’s dietary stance fit in with what Char­lotte Alston describes as an “increas­ing­ly orga­nized” inter­na­tion­al veg­e­tar­i­an move­ment tak­ing shape in the late nine­teenth cen­tu­ry.

Like Tol­stoy in “The First Step,” pro­po­nents of veg­e­tar­i­an­ism argued not only against cru­el­ty to ani­mals, but also against “the bru­tal­iza­tion of those who worked in the meat indus­try, as butch­ers, slaugh­ter­men, and even shep­herds and drovers.” But veg­e­tar­i­an­ism was only one part of Tolstoy’s reli­gious phi­los­o­phy, which also includ­ed chasti­ty, tem­per­ance, the rejec­tion of pri­vate prop­er­ty, and “a com­plete refusal to par­tic­i­pate in vio­lence or coer­cion of any kind.” This marked his dietary prac­tice as dis­tinct from many con­tem­po­raries. Tol­stoy and his fol­low­ers “made the link between veg­e­tar­i­an­ism and a wider human­i­tar­i­an­ism explic­it.”

“How was it pos­si­ble,” Alston sum­ma­rizes, “to regard the killing of ani­mals for food as evil, but not to con­demn the killing of men through war and cap­i­tal pun­ish­ment? Not all mem­bers of the veg­e­tar­i­an move­ment agreed.” Some saw “no con­nec­tion between the ques­tions of war and diet.” Tolstoy’s philo­soph­i­cal argu­ment against all forms of vio­lence was not orig­i­nal to him, but it res­onat­ed all over the world with those who saw him as a shin­ing exam­ple, includ­ing his two daugh­ters and even­tu­al­ly his wife Sophia, who all adopt­ed the prac­tice of veg­e­tar­i­an­ism. A book of their recipes was pub­lished in 1874, and adapt­ed by Pavlenko for his Leo Tol­stoy: A Vegetarian’s Tale. (See one exam­ple here—a fam­i­ly recipe for mac­a­roni and cheese.)

In her study Tol­stoy and His Dis­ci­ples, Alston details the Russ­ian great’s wide influ­ence through not only his diet but the total­i­ty of his spir­i­tu­al prac­tices and unique polit­i­cal and reli­gious views. Inter­est­ing­ly, unlike many ani­mal rights activists of his day and ours, Tol­stoy refused to endorse leg­is­la­tion to pun­ish ani­mal cru­el­ty, believ­ing that pun­ish­ment would only result in the per­pet­u­a­tion of vio­lence. “Non-vio­lence, non-resis­tance and broth­er­hood were the prin­ci­ples that lay at the basis of Tol­stoy­an veg­e­tar­i­an­ism,” she observes, “and while these prin­ci­ples meant that Tol­stoy­ans coop­er­at­ed close­ly with veg­e­tar­i­ans, they also kept them in many ways apart.”

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

entries.title: When Animals Were Put on Trial in Medieval Europe
entries.summary: Most of us twenty-first-century urbanites have a fairly sentimental view of farm animals, precisely because so many generations have gone by since they’ve been part of our daily lives. (In South Korea, where I live, the agricultural past remains just within living memory. Perhaps that’s why so many restaurants in Seoul advertise their meat with […]
entries.content:
Most of us twen­ty-first-cen­tu­ry urban­ites have a fair­ly sen­ti­men­tal view of farm ani­mals, pre­cise­ly because so many gen­er­a­tions have gone by since they’ve been part of our dai­ly lives. (In South Korea, where I live, the agri­cul­tur­al past remains just with­in liv­ing mem­o­ry. Per­haps that’s why so many restau­rants in Seoul adver­tise their meat with pic­tures of the ani­mals it comes from, some­times dressed in chef’s garb and cheer­ful­ly serv­ing up the very dish­es they’re about to become.) Things were dif­fer­ent in medieval Europe, where ani­mals were both a neces­si­ty and a poten­tial dan­ger. His­to­ry records many instances of seri­ous harm done to humans by hors­es, bulls, and espe­cial­ly pigs, who seem to have had a par­tic­u­lar ten­den­cy to turn on chil­dren.

Today we would describe the killing of a child as an inhu­man act, a term that, in these cas­es, applies more than fig­u­ra­tive­ly. As for the fate of the vio­lent­ly offend­ing ani­mal, we might imag­ine that it would be sum­mar­i­ly slaugh­tered, but between the tenth and eigh­teenth cen­turies — and espe­cial­ly in the fif­teenth and six­teenth cen­turies — it might well have been brought into a court­room first. Though oth­er crea­tures had already been sub­ject to legal pro­ceed­ings for quite some time, “the ear­li­est record­ed pig tri­al took place in Fonte­nay-aux-Ros­es, just out­side Paris, in 1266,” writes Alexan­der Lee at His­to­ry Today. “By the ear­ly fif­teenth cen­tu­ry, how­ev­er, they had become estab­lished prac­tice through­out Nor­mandy and the Île-de-France,” even­tu­al­ly spread­ing beyond the bor­der to Italy, Ger­many, and the Low Coun­tries.

“As con­tem­po­rary stu­dents of the Cor­pus iuris civilis knew, it was a basic prin­ci­ple of Roman law that ani­mals could not be cul­pa­ble,” Lee adds. “Lack­ing rea­son, they were inca­pable of har­bor­ing crim­i­nal intent and hence could not be guilty of a crime.” But in un-Roman north­ern France, “the admin­is­tra­tion of sec­u­lar jus­tice was still large­ly the con­cern of local seigneurs and was gov­erned pre­dom­i­nant­ly by cus­tom rather than statute.” Thus sus­tained, ani­mal tri­als served pur­pos­es beyond sim­ple pun­ish­ment. “For medieval peo­ple, the world was cre­at­ed by God in a very log­i­cal way, with ani­mals cre­at­ed first, in order to serve and help human beings who were cre­at­ed in the image of God,” says Uni­ver­si­ty of Liv­er­pool medieval Euro­pean mon­ster expert Dami­an Kempf, quot­ed in Pop­u­lar Sci­ence by Anne Ewbank. In that world­view, try­ing and exe­cut­ing a pig could “restore what was bro­ken.”

Unlike domes­tic ani­mals, accord­ing to Sonya Vatom­sky at JSTOR Dai­ly, destruc­tive mice, bee­tles, snails, wee­vils, and oth­er ver­min would be sent to eccle­si­as­ti­cal tri­bunals. “Despite being unlike­ly can­di­dates for Catholi­cism, such crea­tures were pun­ished with excom­mu­ni­ca­tion, not exe­cu­tion,” she writes, since cast­ing them out of God’s domain would allow humans to exter­mi­nate them with peace of mind. Vatom­sky also quotes econ­o­mist Peter T. Leeson’s the­o­ry that the Catholic Church tried more ani­mals when peo­ple got lax about tithing, with the aim of “bol­ster­ing cit­i­zens’ belief in the valid­i­ty of Church pun­ish­ments for tithe eva­sion.” Putting ani­mals on tri­al may now strike us as grotesque, but like any alien-seem­ing episode of his­to­ry, it also reveals the beliefs on which a past soci­ety oper­at­ed — a mode of analy­sis that gets one won­der­ing how far the mod­ern Unit­ed States is from giv­ing them the right to sue.

entries.content:
Taught by his­to­ri­an Mar­ci Shore, “Euro­pean Intel­lec­tu­al His­to­ry Since Niet­zsche” sur­veys the sto­ry of mod­ern thought, from the late 18th cen­tu­ry to the late 20th.

Along the way, the course explores major trends in mod­ern Euro­pean thought: Marx­ism-Lenin­ism, psy­cho­analy­sis, expres­sion­ism, struc­tural­ism, phe­nom­e­nol­o­gy, exis­ten­tial­ism, anti-pol­i­tics, and decon­struc­tion. Intel­lec­tu­al fig­ures cov­ered in the course include Niet­zsche, Lenin, Kaf­ka, Freud, Husserl, de Beau­voir, Hei­deg­ger, Arendt, Adorno, Sartre, Girard, Fou­cault, Der­ri­da, and Hav­el.

You can watch all 25 lec­tures above. Or find them on YouTube and Apple Pod­casts. Explore the course hand­outs here.

“Euro­pean Intel­lec­tu­al His­to­ry Since Niet­zsche” will be added to our col­lec­tion, 1,700 Free Online Cours­es from Top Uni­ver­si­ties.

entries.title: 2,800-Year-Old Bone Flute Unearthed in Troy May Have Been Played During Homer’s Time
entries.summary: Image by Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, via Twitter The prolific Hans Zimmer scored Christopher Nolan’s films over the dozen years from Batman Begins through Dunkirk. From 2020’s Tenet onward, Nolan has employed the younger Swedish composer Ludwig Göransson. Just what difference this has made in the resulting pictures is a matter best left to the scrutiny of the most obsessive […]
entries.content:
Image by Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, via Twit­ter

The pro­lif­ic Hans Zim­mer scored Christo­pher Nolan’s films over the dozen years from Bat­man Begins through Dunkirk. From 2020’s Tenet onward, Nolan has employed the younger Swedish com­pos­er Lud­wig Görans­son. Just what dif­fer­ence this has made in the result­ing pic­tures is a mat­ter best left to the scruti­ny of the most obses­sive fans, but any view­er can hear how much Zim­mer and Görans­son dif­fer styl­is­ti­cal­ly. This past sum­mer, the siren song includ­ed on the sound­track of The Odyssey fea­tured one of the lat­ter’s par­tic­u­lar­ly notable choic­es: the use of an aulos, a dou­ble-reed­ed wind instru­ment much played back in ancient Greece.

Though Görans­son did­n’t have a gen­uine­ly ancient aulos on hand, of course, the sound pro­duced by the repli­ca proved evoca­tive enough. But just this year, as it hap­pens, a bone flute actu­al­ly dat­ing from the peri­od in which Homer wrote The Odyssey was unearthed from the archae­o­log­i­cal site of ancient Troy in mod­ern-day north­west­ern Turkey.

As Smithsonian.com’s Meilan Sol­ly writes, the past 160 years of dig­ging there have pro­duced “a pair of gold diadems, more than 100 two-han­dled wine gob­lets, and arrow­heads and weapons dat­ed to the Late Bronze Age, among oth­er arti­facts.” This 2,800-year-old flute isn’t just the first musi­cal instru­ment dis­cov­ered at the site, but also fur­ther evi­dence that Troy was­n’t the ghost town it was once assumed to be in the eighth cen­tu­ry BC.

As always when deal­ing with ancient arti­facts — and espe­cial­ly ones, as these pic­tures reveal, in a less-than-whole state — we should be care­ful with our terms. “Call­ing the object a flute is the exca­va­tors’ choice of word, and the type remains open,” says Ancient Ori­gins. While this new dis­cov­ery could poten­tial­ly be a real Greek aulos, “with­out hole counts or a pub­lished draw­ing, match­ing the Troy find to that design is pre­ma­ture.” Archae­ol­o­gists have unearthed sim­i­lar instru­ments else­where, dat­ing from dif­fer­ent peri­ods, but nev­er before has one emerged from the buried remains of a city so rich in leg­endary asso­ci­a­tions. To those in search of a deep­er under­stand­ing of antiq­ui­ty, the site con­tin­ues to sound a siren song of its own.

entries.title: When Salvador Dali Met Sigmund Freud, and Changed Freud’s Mind About Surrealism (1938)
entries.summary: The close associations between Surrealism and Freudian psychoanalysis were liberally encouraged by the most famous proponent of the movement, Salvador Dalí, who considered himself a devoted follower of Freud. We don’t have to wonder what the founder of psychoanalysis would have thought of his self-appointed protégé. We have them recording, in their own words, their […]
entries.content:
The close asso­ci­a­tions between Sur­re­al­ism and Freudi­an psy­cho­analy­sis were lib­er­al­ly encour­aged by the most famous pro­po­nent of the move­ment, Sal­vador Dalí, who con­sid­ered him­self a devot­ed fol­low­er of Freud. We don’t have to won­der what the founder of psy­cho­analy­sis would have thought of his self-appoint­ed pro­tégé.

We have them record­ing, in their own words, their impres­sions of their one and only meeting—which took place in July of 1938, at Freud’s home in Lon­don. Freud was 82, Dalí 34. We also have sketch­es Dalí made of Freud while the two sat togeth­er. Their mem­o­ries of events, shall we say, dif­fer con­sid­er­ably, or at least they seemed total­ly bewil­dered by each oth­er. (Freud pro­nounced Dalí a “fanat­ic.”)

In any case, there’s absolute­ly no way the encounter could have lived up to Dalí’s expec­ta­tions, as the Freud Muse­um Lon­don notes:

[Dalí] had already trav­elled to Vien­na sev­er­al times but failed to make an intro­duc­tion. Instead, he wrote in his auto­bi­og­ra­phy, he spent his time hav­ing “long and exhaus­tive imag­i­nary con­ver­sa­tions” with his hero, at one point fan­ta­siz­ing that he “came home with me and stayed all night cling­ing to the cur­tains of my room in the Hotel Sach­er.”

Freud was cer­tain­ly not going to indulge Dalí’s pecu­liar fan­tasies, but what the artist real­ly want­ed was val­i­da­tion of his work—and maybe his very being. “Dalí had spent his teens and ear­ly twen­ties read­ing Freud’s works on the uncon­scious,” writes Paul Gal­lagher at Dan­ger­ous Minds, “on sex­u­al­i­ty and The Inter­pre­ta­tion of Dreams.” He was obsessed. Final­ly meet­ing Freud in ’38, he must have felt “like a believ­er might feel when com­ing face-to-face with God.”

He brought with him his lat­est paint­ing The Meta­mor­pho­sis of Nar­cis­sus, and an arti­cle he had pub­lished on para­noia. This, espe­cial­ly, Dalí hoped would gain the respect of the elder­ly Freud.

Try­ing to inter­est him, I explained that it was not a sur­re­al­ist diver­sion, but was real­ly an ambi­tious­ly sci­en­tif­ic arti­cle, and I repeat­ed the title, point­ing to it at the same time with my fin­ger. Before his imper­turbable indif­fer­ence, my voice became invol­un­tar­i­ly sharp­er and more insis­tent.

On being shown the paint­ing, Freud sup­pos­ed­ly said, “in clas­sic paint­ings I look for the uncon­scious, but in your paint­ings I look for the con­scious.” The com­ment stung, though Dalí wasn’t entire­ly sure what it meant. But he took it as fur­ther evi­dence that the meet­ing was a bust. Sketch­ing Freud in the draw­ing below, he wrote, “Freud’s cra­ni­um is a snail! His brain is in the form of a spiral—to be extract­ed with a nee­dle!”

One might see why Freud was sus­pi­cious of Sur­re­al­ists, “who have appar­ent­ly cho­sen me as their patron saint,” he wrote to Ste­fan Zweig, the mutu­al friend who intro­duced him to Dalí. In 1921, poet and Sur­re­al­ist man­i­festo writer André Bre­ton “had shown up unin­vit­ed on [Freud’s] doorstep.” Unhap­py with his recep­tion, Bre­ton pub­lished a “bit­ter attack,” call­ing Freud an “old man with­out ele­gance” and lat­er accused Freud of pla­gia­riz­ing him.

Despite the mem­o­ry of this nas­ti­ness, and Freud’s gen­er­al dis­taste for mod­ern art, he could­n’t help but be impressed with Dalí. “Until then,” he wrote to Zweig, “I was inclined to look upon the sur­re­al­ists… as absolute (let us say 95 per­cent, like alco­hol), cranks. That young Spaniard, how­ev­er, with his can­did and fanat­i­cal eyes, and his unde­ni­able tech­ni­cal mas­tery, has made me recon­sid­er my opin­ion.”

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2020.

Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

entries.title: Watch Seoul’s 6,500-Year Evolution in a Mesmerizing 3D Animated Time Lapse
entries.summary: In this century, few countries have been as visibly successful as South Korea. China’s vertiginous economic rise once absorbed vast amounts of news-media attention, but its soft power has comparatively little reach across the wider world, at least in English-speaking countries. By this point, many if not most Westerners haven’t just eaten Korean food, but […]
entries.content:
In this cen­tu­ry, few coun­tries have been as vis­i­bly suc­cess­ful as South Korea. Chi­na’s ver­tig­i­nous eco­nom­ic rise once absorbed vast amounts of news-media atten­tion, but its soft pow­er has com­par­a­tive­ly lit­tle reach across the wider world, at least in Eng­lish-speak­ing coun­tries. By this point, many if not most West­ern­ers haven’t just eat­en Kore­an food, but also dri­ven a Kore­an car, heard Kore­an pop music, or watched a Kore­an film or TV show. The result­ing sense of famil­iar­i­ty can prove decep­tive to those who even­tu­al­ly make the trip there, but it does, at least, mark an improve­ment on the scant knowl­edge of the place they had before. Not so long ago, they could say lit­tle with cer­tain­ty except this: South Kore­a’s got Seoul.

I first saw that pun on a T‑shirt in high school, long before I knew much of any­thing about Korea myself. Now, hav­ing lived there for more than a decade, I’ve been able to watch from the inside as the coun­try’s cap­i­tal has become an unlike­ly object of gen­er­al inter­est. As evi­dence, take the 1.2 mil­lion views already racked up by the new video from Latos Charts above, a 3D ani­mat­ed time lapse show­ing the evo­lu­tion of Seoul over six and a half often tumul­tuous mil­len­nia.

It reveals, among oth­er things, that the city did­n’t exist for most of the his­to­ry of Kore­an civ­i­liza­tion — but then, nei­ther did the coun­try. The post­war divi­sion of the penin­su­la into North and South has a kind of prece­dent in the war­ring king­doms that occu­pied it before its uni­fi­ca­tion by a series of states cul­mi­nat­ing in the 500-year rule of the Joseon Dynasty.

If you’ve watched one of the many pop­u­lar his­tor­i­cal “K‑dramas,” Joseon was most like­ly its peri­od set­ting. Now gen­er­al­ly regard­ed as the pre­de­ces­sor of mod­ern-day Korea, it pass­es in two min­utes of the time lapse, dur­ing which Seoul, then known as Hanyang, takes amid its geo­man­ti­cal­ly pro­tec­tive moun­tains more or less the shape it has today, at least north of the Han Riv­er. In fact, up until the sev­en­ties, there was no city to speak of south of the Han: the devel­op­ment of the more recent­ly musi­cal­ly sat­i­rized Gang­nam, lit­er­al­ly “south of the riv­er,” was part of the top-down push for eco­nom­ic devel­op­ment — in effect, hit­ting the fast-for­ward but­ton on his­to­ry — that fol­lowed the dev­as­ta­tion of the Kore­an War. That chap­ter of his­to­ry comes around eight min­utes into the video, after which looka­like high-rise com­plex­es start pop­ping up like mush­rooms after a mon­soon.

How­ev­er com­fort­able a lifestyle they’ve offered to mid­dle-class Seoulites, the sight of those apa­teu dan­ji unset­tles some West­ern observers, who encounter them in pho­tographs meant to depict the city as a kind of futur­is­tic dystopia. They exag­ger­ate, of course, but even some­one who appre­ci­ates Seoul as much as I do has to admit that, along­side its impres­sive qual­i­ties — the mag­nif­i­cent sub­way sys­tem, for exam­ple, extolled in the Not Just Bikes video above — the city has its prob­lems, as does the nation for which it stands. Under­stand­ing it in all its com­plex­i­ty requires first (even before learn­ing the Kore­an lan­guage) grasp­ing its sheer cen­tral­i­ty, greater than Toky­o’s to Japan or even Paris’ to France. To a great extent, South Korea has­n’t just got Seoul, it is Seoul. And maybe, if its promi­nence in the wider world con­tin­ues to grow, the pun­ning will even­tu­al­ly stop. In Kore­an his­to­ry, stranger things have cer­tain­ly hap­pened.

entries.title: Inspiration from Charles Bukowski: You Might Be Old, Your Life May Be “Crappy,” But You Can Still Make Good Art
entries.summary: Now more than ever, there’s tremendous pressure to make it big while you’re young. Pity the 31-year-old who fails to make it onto a 30-under-30 list… The soon-to-graduate high schooler passed over for YouTube stardom… The great hordes who creep into middle age without so much as a TED Talk to their names… Social media definitely […]
entries.content:
Now more than ever, there’s tremen­dous pres­sure to make it big while you’re young.

Pity the 31-year-old who fails to make it onto a 30-under-30 list…

The soon-to-grad­u­ate high school­er passed over for YouTube star­dom…

The great hordes who creep into mid­dle age with­out so much as a TED Talk to their names…

Social media def­i­nite­ly mag­ni­fies the sen­sa­tion that an unac­cept­able num­ber of our peers have been grant­ed first-class cab­ins aboard a ship that’s sailed with­out us. If we weren’t so demor­al­ized, we’d sue Insta­gram for cre­at­ing the impres­sion that every­one else’s per­fect­ly fil­tered life is lead­ing to book deals and pro­files in The New York­er.

Don’t despair, dear read­er. Charles Bukows­ki is about to make your day from beyond the grave.

In 1993, at the age of 73, the late writer and self-described “spoiled old toad,” took a break from record­ing the audio­book of Run With the Hunt­ed to reflect upon his “crap­py” life.

Some of these thoughts made it into Drew Christie’s ani­ma­tion, above, a reminder that the smoothest road isn’t always nec­es­sar­i­ly the rich­est one.

In ser­vice of his ill-pay­ing muse, Bukows­ki logged decades in unglam­orous jobs—dishwasher, truck dri­ver and loader, gas sta­tion atten­dant, stock boy, ware­house­man, ship­ping clerk, park­ing lot atten­dant, Red Cross order­ly, ele­va­tor oper­a­tor, and most noto­ri­ous­ly, postal car­ri­er and clerk. These gigs gave him plen­ty of mate­r­i­al, the sort of real world expe­ri­ence that eludes those upon whom lit­er­ary fame and for­tune smiles ear­ly.

(His alco­holic mis­ad­ven­tures pro­vid­ed yet more mate­r­i­al, earn­ing him such hon­orifics as the “poet lau­re­ate of L.A. lowlife” and “enfant ter­ri­ble of the Meat School poets.”)

One might also take com­fort in hear­ing a writer as prodi­gious as Bukows­ki reveal­ing that he didn’t hold him­self to the sort of dai­ly writ­ing reg­i­men that can be dif­fi­cult to achieve when one is jug­gling day jobs, stu­dent loans, and/or a fam­i­ly. Also appre­ci­at­ed is the far-from-cur­so­ry nod he accords the ther­a­peu­tic ben­e­fits that are avail­able to all those who write, regard­less of any pub­lic or finan­cial recog­ni­tion:

Three or four nights out of sev­en. If I don’t get those in, I don’t act right. I feel sick. I get very depressed. It’s a release. It’s my psy­chi­a­trist, let­ting this shit out. I’m lucky I get paid for it. I’d do it for noth­ing. In fact, I’d pay to do it. Here, I’ll give you ten thou­sand a year if you’ll let me write.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.
